access_status: Open HTML text retrieved (HTTP 200; source lines name MIKK 1973 and 1969)

tradition: Multilingual pass: Persian, Arabic, Ottoman, Chagatai and Tatar

evidence_text: compilation of oral and written legend (Chinggisid tribal origins with tamghas, uran and tree, abridged from Rashid al-Din and Abu'l-Ghazi according to the catalogue; Timur's destruction of Bulghar; Kazan lore); retrospective, not historical in the modern sense (the BnF cataloguer calls it 'sans valeur historique')

The Kazan 1819/1822 print (Daftar-i Chingiz-nama) and Ivanics and Usmanov's 2002 edition were not found online. | | Also recorded independently by the russian pass: Open web text retrieved (https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/M.Asien/XVIII/1720-1740/Daftar_i_chingiz_name/text1.phtml?id=13830). | Further copies: https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/zolotoord.html
research_value: The Volga-Tatar folk-historical tradition on Chinggis Khan, Timur and the fall of Bulghar; this is the popular Tatar memory of 'Tartary' as opposed to the Persian court histories, and the Kazan 1822 print made it one of the first Tatar-language printed histories.

creator: Mahmud al-Kashgari (fl. 1072-1077)

creator: Yusuf Khass Hajib (fl. 1069-1070)
title: Wisdom of Royal Glory: Qarakhanid Turkic mirror for princes, 1069-1070; Vambery's 1870 partial edition of the Vienna (Herat 1439) Uyghur-script manuscript with German translation, and a facsimile of the Fergana (Namangan) manuscript

research_value: Together with Kashgari, the Qarakhanid literary evidence that a Turkic Islamic state existed in the Tarim-Semirechye region in the 1070s, the region European maps later filled with 'Tartary'.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text (Vambery copies); open PDF (Fergana facsimile)

creator: Second Turk qaghanate court (Yollugh Tegin; Tonyukuk)
title: The Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions (732, 735, c.726) and Yenisei inscriptions: Radloff's editions with transcription and German translation (St Petersburg 1894-1899) and Thomsen's decipherment and French translation (Helsingfors 1896); Finnish 1892 atlas of squeezes
original_script_title: Orkhon inscriptions (Kul Tegin, Bilge Qaghan, Tonyukuk)
tradition: Multilingual pass: Persian, Arabic, Ottoman, Chagatai and Tatar
language: Old Turkic (runiform, transcribed) with German (Radloff) and French (Thomsen) translations; Chinese (original: Old Turkic)
regions_text: Orkhon valley (Mongolia); Yenisei (Tuva, Khakassia); the steppe from the Khingan to the Iron Gate (Temir Qapigh) as named in the texts
peoples_text: Turks (Kok Turk); Toquz Oghuz; Uyghurs; Kirghiz; Qurıqan; Otuz Tatar (the earliest occurrence of the name Tatar); Khitan; Tatabi; Tang China; Sogdians; Turgesh
evidence_text: official record: contemporary royal funerary inscriptions of the Turk qaghanate, in Old Turkic runiform script with a Chinese text on the Kul Tegin stele; the earliest self-designation 'Turk' and the earliest Turkic-language description of the steppe polities (Toquz Oghuz, Qirqiz, Qurıqan, Otuz Tatar, Qitany, Tatabi)
cautions: Readings of 1894-1896 are superseded (Tekin 1968, Berta 2004, Aydin 2012) but the editions remain the base; Radloff and Thomsen disagreed on many readings. The Chinese face of the Kul Tegin stele (732) is a separate Tang text. | Uyghur (Turfan) documents: only F. W. K. Mueller's Uigurica (IA Muller_uigurica, 1908) was located; Radloff's Uigurische Sprachdenkmaeler (1928) not found open. Left as a gap. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/worterverzeichnisienissei (Donner 1892 Yenisei glossary)
research_value: The one class of steppe source with fixed dates and provenance: dated eighth-century monuments in which the Turks name themselves, their neighbours (including the 'Thirty Tatars') and their empire's extent, independent of Chinese or Islamic mediation. They are the terminus a quo for the name 'Tatar' in a Turkic-language document.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved (metadata checked)

creator: Vincent of Beauvais; Simon of Saint-Quentin (excerpted source)

peoples_text: Tartars; Mongols; Baiju; Guyuk; Seljuks of Rum; Georgians; Armenians

Incunable and 1494 copies exist on IA (A336104) for comparison.
research_value: Only surviving witness to Simon of Saint-Quentin's Historia Tartarorum, the Dominican counterpart to Carpini's Franciscan report, covering the Mongol army in Armenia and Persia in the 1240s; also the vehicle by which Carpini's text circulated in the Middle Ages.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (11 MB djvu.txt)

creator: Brother C. de Bridia
title: History of the Tartars (the 'Tartar Relation'), Beinecke MS 350A.1

creator: Matthew Paris; H. R. Luard, editor
title: Chronica majora (Greater Chronicle), volumes III (1216-1239) and IV (1240-1247): the Mongol/Tartar notices and inserted letters of 1238-1247
tradition: Multilingual pass: Latin, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese
regions_text: Hungary; Poland; Rus; Caspian region ('Caspian mountains'); Holy Land; Cathay/Tartary as reported
peoples_text: Tartars (Tattari, Tatari); Mongols; Hungarians; Cumans; Russians; Saracens; Frederick II
evidence_text: compilation and informant testimony: St Albans chronicler recording rumours and copying letters (Ivo of Narbonne 1243, Frederick II 1241, Peter the Russian archbishop's 1244 deposition, Hungarian and Dominican letters) received in England
cautions: Matthew copies documents of uncertain provenance (Ivo of Narbonne letter is a contested text); his own commentary mixes apocalyptic tropes (Gog and Magog) with reportage. Luard's text is standard but pre-modern.
research_value: The principal English-based Latin chronicle recording how news of the Mongol invasion reached Western Europe, including the earliest use of the Tartarus etymology and the letters that defined 'Tartar' for Latin Europe; essential for the name's history.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved for both volumes

creator: Master Roger of Torre Maggiore, archdeacon of Várad (Oradea); Jacques Bongars, editor
title: Sorrowful Lament on the Destruction of the Kingdom of Hungary by the Tartars (Carmen miserabile), in Bongars's Hungarian historians collection
tradition: Multilingual pass: Latin, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese
regions_text: Hungary (Great Plain, Várad, Transylvania, Danube); Pest; Esztergom
peoples_text: Tartars (Mongols under Batu, Kadan); Hungarians (Béla IV); Cumans (Köten); Germans; Ruthenians
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Rogerius was captured by the Mongols in 1241 and lived among them in occupied Hungary until 1242; written c. 1243-1244 and addressed to Bishop James of Palestrina
cautions: Textual transmission entirely via the 1488 Thuroczy prints (no MS); modern critical edition Juhász in Scriptores rerum Hungaricarum II (1938) and Bak/Rady CEMT 5 (2010) not open access. The Bongars 1600 volume also contains Thuroczy and other Hungarian chronicles with Tartar notices.
research_value: The most detailed contemporary eyewitness account of Mongol administration in a conquered European kingdom (census, appointed officials, harvest under occupation), and of the withdrawal of 1242; central for what 'Tartar' rule looked like on the ground.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved for both 1600 and 1488 printings

creator: Thomas, archdeacon of Split; Ivan Lučić (Giovanni Lucio), editor
title: History of the Bishops of Salona and Split, chapters 36-40 on the Tartars (first printed edition, in Lucius, On the Kingdom of Dalmatia and Croatia)
tradition: Multilingual pass: Latin, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese
regions_text: Dalmatia (Split, Trogir, Klis); Hungary; Croatia; Ruthenia (reported)

evidence_text: firsthand observation for 1241-1242: Thomas witnessed King Béla IV's flight to Split and Trogir and the Mongol pursuit along the Dalmatian coast; includes an ethnographic chapter 'De natura Tartarorum'

research_value: Independent Dalmatian eyewitness of the 1241-1242 Mongol invasion, with a description of Tartar appearance, weapons and tactics, and of the pursuit of the Hungarian king to the Adriatic; complements Rogerius.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved

creator: Hayton of Corycus (Het'um), Armenian prince and Premonstratensian; Charles Kohler, editor

type: geography / diplomatic journal (Hanoverian resident's account) with appended documents
regions_text: Russia; St Petersburg; Siberia (reports); Caspian; Volga
peoples_text: Russian Empire; Kalmyks; Siberian peoples; Bashkirs; Persia
evidence_text: mixed: firsthand observation in St Petersburg 1714-1719 combined with documents and reports obtained from others, including material on Siberia and the Kalmyks and an appended account of Peter's Persian and Caspian projects
cautions: Published anonymously; Weber's authorship is standard attribution. Parts 2-3 appeared after his death and contain compiled documents. Multiple BSB copies and a 1744 reissue exist on IA. | English translation The Present State of Russia (1722-1723) exists but is not in the English pass. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/10691836bsb
research_value: Standard German contemporary source on Petrine Russia; part 1 appends reports on Siberia and the Swedish captives, and Weber transmits early news of the Kalmyks, Bukhara expeditions (Bekovich-Cherkassky) and the Caspian; used by Strahlenberg's readers as context.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text available for all three parts (metadata verified; text not sampled)

creator: Anonymous (Nuremberg compiler); includes Johann Bernhard Müller
title: The Very Latest State of Siberia, a great and hitherto little-known Muscovite province in Asia: its government, land, mountains, animals, rivers, towns, and the customs of the Samoyeds, Voguls, Kalmyks, Ostyaks, Tunguses, Buryats, Mongols and other Tatar peoples, with a historical report on the Swedish prisoners in this land, the school at Tobolsk and the beginning of the conversion of the heathen
type: geography / compilation with embedded firsthand ethnographic report

date.subject_text: c. 1711-1719 (Swedish captivity in Tobolsk; Müller among the Ostyaks 1712-1716)

regions_text: Siberia; Tobolsk; Ob basin; Irtysh; Kalmyk steppe; Mongolia frontier
peoples_text: Samoyeds; Voguls; Kalmyks; Ostyaks; Tunguses; Buryats; Mongols; Siberian Tatars; Swedish captives
evidence_text: compilation of recent reports (Swedish captives in Tobolsk, Pietist correspondence) including Müller's firsthand description of the Ostyaks written 1716 at Tobolsk
cautions: Anonymous compilation; J. B. Müller's Ostyak account is the core firsthand piece and was separately printed (Berlin 1720) and translated (Weber 1722-1723 English). Preface signals dependence on Dutch manuscript material (Witsen). | Catalogue gives no author; the OCR preface refers to a Dutch work preserved only in manuscript, presumably Witsen.
research_value: Earliest German printed ethnography of Siberian peoples, built from Swedish captives' reports; title lists the Tatar peoples of Siberia individually, a useful contemporary usage of Tartarische Völker as a collective label.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (283 images)

creator: Lorenz Lange; P. S. Pallas (ed.)
title: Journal of Two Journeys made in 1727, 1728 and 1736 from Kiakhta and Tsurukhaitu through Mongolia to Peking, with a geographical-historical description of the city of Peking
type: travel narrative / caravan and embassy journal
language: German (original: German (Lange wrote in German; some journals survive in Russian and French versions))
regions_text: Mongolia (Gobi route); Kiakhta; Tsurukhaitu (Argun frontier); Beijing
peoples_text: Mongols (Khalkha); Qing China; Russian caravan trade; Zunghars mentioned
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Lange led Russian caravans to Beijing; edited posthumously by Pallas from manuscripts
cautions: Lange's earlier 1715-1717 and 1721-1722 journals were printed in Weber's Das veränderte Russland and in Bell; this 1781 volume prints the later journals. Pallas as editor may have abridged. | IA bub_gb_rWABAAAAQAAJ is mislabelled English in catalogue; the text is German.
research_value: Eyewitness Gobi crossings between the Kiakhta treaty frontier and Beijing, complementing Lange's earlier journal known in English only through Bell (W001) and Weber; describes Mongol posts, Qing frontier control and the caravan trade.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (163 images)

creator: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (ed.)
title: Collection of Russian History (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte), 9 volumes in 54 parts, St Petersburg 1732-1764; contains Müller's Siberian history, the Nachrichten von Seereisen (1758), pieces on the Kalmyks, Samoyeds, Yugra, the Amur and Chinese-Russian relations
type: compilation / retrospective history / scientific report (Academy serial)

date.subject_text: 1733-1743 (Müller's Siberian archive survey and travels); earlier events from documents

regions_text: Siberia; Kamchatka; Amur; Arctic coast; Kalmyk steppe; Yugra; Bering Strait; Volga
peoples_text: Siberian Tatars (Kuchum's khanate); Kalmyks; Samoyeds; Yakuts; Chukchi; Kamchadals; Zunghars; Qing China; Muscovy
evidence_text: mixed: retrospective history from Siberian archival documents Müller copied 1733-1743 (Sibirische Geschichte, vols 6 and 8), firsthand and informant material from the Second Kamchatka Expedition, and edited reports of others
cautions: Serial with several contributors; individual pieces variously by Müller, Fischer, Steller and others; a 1777-1779 Offenbach reprint (IA 11249233bsb etc., sammlungrussisc00unkngoog) rearranges content. Russian Istoriia Sibiri (IA istoriya_sibiri_vol_1) is the later edition of Müller's Russian text. | The English pass has Coxe (W086) and Conquest of Siberia (1842, IA conquestsiberia00pallgoog) which derive from this serial. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/mullergfsammlungrussischergeschichte0; https://archive.org/details/mullergfsammlungrussischergeschichte90; https://archive.org/details/mullergfsammlungrussischergeschichte46; https://archive.org/details/mullergfsammlungrussischergeschichte38; https://archive.org/details/mullergfsammlungrussischergeschichte24; https://archive.org/details/11249233bsb
research_value: Foundation of Siberian historiography: Müller's history of the conquest of the Siberian khanate from Tobolsk and other archives, the Nachrichten von Seereisen (Bering, Dezhnev), essays on Kalmyk, Samoyed and Yugra questions and on the Amur. Central for how eighteenth-century scholars reconstructed pre-Russian Siberia and Tartary from documents rather than travellers' reports.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text for all nine volumes; text sampled in vol. 6 (Fraktur OCR good)

creator: Johann Eberhard Fischer
title: Siberian History from the Discovery of Siberia to the Conquest of this Land by Russian Arms, read in the sessions of the Academy of Sciences, 2 volumes

date.subject_text: 1740-1747 (Fischer in Siberia); events from the sixteenth-seventeenth centuries

regions_text: Siberia; Ural; Ob; Irtysh; Yenisei; Lena; Amur; Kalmyk steppe
peoples_text: Siberian khanate (Kuchum); Tatars; Kalmyks; Ostyaks; Voguls; Tunguses; Buryats; Yakuts; Mongols; Qing China
evidence_text: retrospective history compiled from Müller's archival extracts and Fischer's own participation in the Second Kamchatka Expedition (1740-1747); includes an introduction on the origin of the Tatar, Mongol and Finno-Ugric peoples
cautions: Heavily dependent on Müller's unpublished Russian history; Müller accused Fischer of appropriation. A Russian translation appeared 1774 (IA SibirskajaistorijassamagootkrytijaSibiri12). | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/SibirskajaistorijassamagootkrytijaSibiri12
research_value: The standard eighteenth-century synthesis of the Russian conquest of Siberia and, in its long introduction, an early comparative-ethnographic attempt to sort out who the Tatars, Mongols and Kalmyks were; frequently plagiarizes Müller, so must be read against the Sammlung.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text for both volumes (metadata verified; text sample request returned HTTP 500 once, not retried)

creator: Peter Simon Pallas
title: Collections of Historical Reports on the Mongolian Peoples (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften), 2 parts, 1776 and 1801
type: compilation / ethnography and history (Kalmyk, Mongol, Buryat, Zunghar) with plates
language: German (with Kalmyk and Mongol terms) (original: German)
regions_text: Volga Kalmyk steppe; Zungharia; Mongolia; Transbaikalia; Tibet (Lamaist religion)
peoples_text: Kalmyks (Torghut, Dörbet, Khoshut); Zunghars; Khalkha Mongols; Buryats; Qing China; Tibetan Buddhism
evidence_text: mixed: Pallas's firsthand observation among the Volga Kalmyks and Buryats 1769-1773, informant testimony (Kalmyk priests, Russian officials), translated Kalmyk and Mongol texts, and compilation of earlier Russian records on the Zunghars and the Torghut flight of 1771
cautions: Part 1 catalogued on IA with language Russian in error (text is German). Part 2 IA date 1776 conflicts with the 1801 imprint; record both. Pallas used Bakunin's Kalmyk history and translations by Jährig; attributions inside the text should be checked case by case. | Reprint Graz 1980 exists.
research_value: The most detailed eighteenth-century European account of Kalmyk and Mongol history, law, religion and material culture, including the origin traditions of the Oirats and the history of Zungharia to its destruction by the Qing; a prime witness for how the Mongol peoples described themselves to a European observer, independent of the Tartary label.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved for both parts

creator: Peter Simon Pallas (ed.)
title: New Northern Contributions to Physical and Geographical Description of Lands and Peoples, Natural History and Economy, 7 volumes, 1781-1796 (continued as Neueste nordische Beyträge)
type: compilation / scientific report (serial publishing travel journals, reports and documents)
language: German (original: German (some pieces translated from Russian))
regions_text: Siberia; Altai; Kamchatka; Aleutians; Kalmyk steppe; Kazakh steppe; Caucasus; Mongolia frontier
peoples_text: Kalmyks; Kazakhs; Bashkirs; Buryats; Mongols; Chukchi; Koryaks; Aleuts; Zunghars; Qing China; Bukhara
evidence_text: mixed: edited firsthand journals and reports by Russian officers, naturalists, missionaries and merchants (Lepekhin, Sujew, Rytschkow, Sokolov, Sievers's Altai and Zunghar letters, Kamchatka and Aleutian voyages, Kalmyk pieces), plus Pallas's own essays
cautions: Serial: authorship differs per article; several pieces are translations from Russian official reports. Catalogue volume numbering differs between the RSL, CIHM and Google copies. | Predecessor serial Nordische Beyträge (Büsching) not searched. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/cihm_38273; https://archive.org/details/cihm_38276; https://archive.org/details/cihm_38277; https://archive.org/details/neuenordischebe02beitgoog
research_value: The principal German-language outlet for Siberian, Altai, Central Asian and Pacific field reports between Pallas's Reise and the 1800s; contains Johann Sievers's letters from the Altai and the Zunghar frontier (1790s), documents on the Kirgis-Kaisak (Kazakh) hordes and Kalmyks, and Pallas's commentary. Must be indexed piece by piece.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved (vol 1 sampled); vol 3 of the RSL set has an empty IA item (pallaspsneuenordischebeitrgezurphysik96, no metadata)

creator: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
title: Description of All the Nations of the Russian Empire, their way of life, religion, customs, dwellings, clothing and other remarkable features, 4 parts with coloured plates (part 2: Tatar nations; part 4: Mongolian nations)
regions_text: whole Russian Empire; Volga; Siberia; Kalmyk and Kazakh steppe; Caucasus; Kamchatka
peoples_text: Tatar nations (Kazan, Siberian, Crimean, Nogai, Bashkir, Kirgis-Kaisak, Teleut, Yakut); Mongolian nations (Kalmyk, Buryat, Mongol); Finnic, Samoyed and Tungusic peoples; Caucasian peoples
evidence_text: compilation of Academy expedition results (Pallas, Falck, Lepekhin, Gmelin, Müller, Steller) with Georgi's own observations 1770-1774
cautions: Secondary compilation; Georgi rarely names his sources per entry. English version (IA bim_eighteenth-century_beschreibung-aller-nati_georgi 1780-1783) not in the English pass. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/10691431bsb; https://archive.org/details/10691432bsb
research_value: Codifies the eighteenth-century classification of the empire's peoples into Tatar and Mongol nations with a plate for each; the explicit statement that Tatar and nomad polities are democratic rather than monarchic appears in the sample. Widely translated (English Russia, or a Compleat Historical Account 1780-1783).
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved (four Google items, volume numbers not stated in metadata); text sample from the Tatar nations part

creator: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
title: Observations of a Journey in the Russian Empire in the Year 1772 (and in 1773 and 1774), 2 volumes, with the new map of Lake Baikal
regions_text: Lake Baikal; Transbaikalia; Irkutsk; Barabinsk steppe; Ural; Kazan
peoples_text: Buryats; Tunguses; Siberian Tatars; Bashkirs; Kazakh frontier; Qing frontier
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Georgi travelled with Falck then Pallas, circumnavigated Lake Baikal 1772 and crossed the Barabinsk steppe and Ural
cautions: Partly overlaps with Pallas's Reise for 1772-1773 since they travelled together in stretches.
research_value: Detailed eyewitness ethnography of the Baikal Buryats and of the Irkutsk frontier with Qing Mongolia in the 1770s; includes the first accurate survey of Lake Baikal (separate IA map item neuecartedesbaikalseeswelchebeyumschiffu73).
access_status: Open scans + OCR text available (metadata verified; text not sampled)

creator: Georg Wilhelm Steller
title: Description of the Land of Kamchatka, its inhabitants, their customs, names, way of life and various habits, with many copperplates (posthumous, ed. J. B. Scherer)
regions_text: Kamchatka; Kuril approaches; Okhotsk; northeastern Siberia
peoples_text: Itelmens (Kamchadals); Koryaks; Kuril Ainu; Russian Cossack administration
evidence_text: firsthand observation in Kamchatka 1740-1744 during the Second Kamchatka Expedition; editorial framing by Scherer 1774
cautions: Posthumous edition; Scherer's editing and additions are not always distinguishable from Steller's manuscript. Krasheninnikov used Steller's papers, so the two texts are interdependent.
research_value: Independent German eyewitness counterpart to Krasheninnikov (W007) for Kamchatka, the northeastern edge of what maps still called Tartary; Steller's ethnography of the Itelmens is firsthand and often more critical of Russian rule.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved

creator: Georg Wilhelm Steller
title: G. W. Steller's Journey from Kamchatka to America with Commander-Captain Bering: a companion to his Description of Kamchatka (ed. Pallas)
regions_text: Kamchatka; Bering Sea; Aleutian and Alaskan coast; Bering Island
peoples_text: Aleuts; Itelmens; Chukchi (report); Russian naval expedition
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Steller's journal of Bering's 1741-1742 voyage and wintering on Bering Island
cautions: IA catalogue title misreads Steller as Weller; Pallas edited and annotated the manuscript.
research_value: Marks the eastern terminus of the Siberian source field: eyewitness voyage from Kamchatka to America; useful as a control on eighteenth-century knowledge of the Chukchi and the northeastern limit of Asia.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (137 images)

creator: Johann Peter Falck; J. G. Georgi (ed.)
title: Contributions to the Topographical Knowledge of the Russian Empire, 3 volumes (vol. 1 itinerary Orenburg steppe and Siberia; vol. 3 the peoples: Tatars, Kalmyks, Kirgis-Kaisaks)
type: travel narrative / geography / scientific report (posthumous Academy expedition journal)
regions_text: Volga; Orenburg steppe; Kazakh steppe frontier; Ural; western Siberia (Tobolsk, Barabinsk, Tara); Kolyvan and Altai
peoples_text: Kazakhs (Kirgis-Kaisaks); Bashkirs; Kalmyks; Kazan and Siberian Tatars; Teleuts; Ostyaks; Bukharans in Siberia
evidence_text: firsthand observation 1768-1774 on the Orenburg-Siberian Academy expedition (Falck died 1774 at Kazan); arranged posthumously by Georgi
cautions: Georgi compiled from Falck's incomplete papers and added material; the third volume on peoples overlaps Georgi's own Beschreibung aller Nationen.
research_value: Contains the fullest eighteenth-century German ethnography of the Kirgis-Kaisak hordes and of the Bukharan traders of Siberia, and a systematic topography of the Orenburg frontier line; complements Pallas and Rychkov.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved; OCR of sampled volume poor

creator: Ivan Lepekhin
title: Journal of the Journey through Various Provinces of the Russian Empire (German translation of Dnevnye zapiski, vols 1-2 covering 1768-1769 and 1770)
original_script_title: Дневные записки путешествия ... по разным провинциям Российского государства
type: travel narrative / scientific report (Academy expedition journal, translation)

cautions: Translation; Hase's preface explains the relation to the Russian 1771 first volume. Third German volume (1783) unverified. | Russian original is in the Russian tradition's remit.
research_value: Russian academician's eyewitness journal of the Volga-Ural frontier in the same years as Pallas, available to German readers; documents Bashkir and Kalmyk settlements and the Orenburg line from a Russian participant.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved (vols 1-2); vol 3 of the German (1783) not located on IA

creator: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin
title: Journey through Russia to Investigate the Three Realms of Nature, 4 parts (part 3: journey through northern Persia 1770-1772; part 4: second Persian journey and death in Dagestan captivity, ed. Pallas 1784)
type: travel narrative / scientific report (Academy expedition journal)
regions_text: Don; lower Volga; Astrakhan; Caspian Sea; Gilan; Mazandaran; Dagestan; Terek
peoples_text: Kalmyks; Astrakhan Tatars; Nogais; Turkmens of the eastern Caspian; Persia (Zand period); Dagestani polities (Kaitag, Derbent, Tarku); Don Cossacks

cautions: Part 4 posthumous, compiled by Pallas from Gmelin's papers; title page misnames the author Samuel Georg. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_X5AaAAAAYAAJ
research_value: Primary eyewitness for the Caspian shores, the Astrakhan Kalmyks and Tatars, the Turkmen coast and Dagestan in 1769-1774, the southwestern margin of the steppe world; also a case of a European captive among Caucasian rulers.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved for all four parts (part 3 sampled)

creator: Karl Ludwig Hablizl
title: Physical Description of the Taurida Governorate according to its situation and all three realms of nature (German translation, Hanover and Osnabrück 1789)
type: geography / scientific report (natural history of the Crimea)
regions_text: Crimea (Taurida); Perekop steppe; Kerch
peoples_text: Crimean Tatars (post-annexation); Nogais; Russian administration
evidence_text: firsthand observation by the vice-governor of Taurida 1784-1785; official survey
cautions: Translation from Russian; mainly natural history, Tatar society treated briefly.
research_value: First systematic post-annexation survey of the Crimean peninsula, the former Crimean Khanate; German access to Russian official knowledge of Little Tartary in the 1780s.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (413 images)

creator: Benjamin Bergmann
title: Benjamin Bergmann's Nomadic Wanderings among the Kalmyks in the Years 1802 and 1803, 4 parts (Riga 1804-1805), including translations of the Kalmyk epic Dschangar, the Geser cycle, Kalmyk law and the history of the Torghut flight of 1771
type: travel narrative / ethnography / compilation (with translated Kalmyk texts)
language: German (with Kalmyk texts in translation) (original: German)
regions_text: Volga Kalmyk steppe; Sarepta; Astrakhan; Zungharia (historical)
peoples_text: Kalmyks (Torghut, Dörbet); Zunghars; Mongols; Qing China (historical); Tibetan Buddhism
evidence_text: mixed: firsthand residence among the Volga Kalmyks 1802-1803 with informant testimony from Kalmyk clergy and nobles; translations of Kalmyk literary and legal texts; retrospective history of the Kalmyks and of the 1771 exodus
cautions: Bergmann's Kalmyk was imperfect; translations were mediated by informants. IA Google copy bub_gb_LmQFAAAAQAAJ mislabelled English. | IA also has two excerpt items (bergman-b.-nomadische-streifereien... Bd. II pp. 205-217; Bd. IV pp. 184-214) posted separately. | Further copies: https://archive.org/details/india.history.resource.110619
research_value: The most intimate pre-1850 German account of Kalmyk society, and the first European rendering of the Dschangar epic and Geser material; preserves Kalmyk oral history of Zungharia and the 1771 migration. Also the German original behind the 1825 French translation.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved for part 1; parts 2-4 metadata verified

creator: Julius von Klaproth
title: Asia Polyglotta (Paris 1823; 2nd ed. 1831), with the Sprachatlas: comparative vocabularies and ethnogenealogical classification of the peoples of Asia (Mongols, Tungus, Turks, Samoyeds, Finns, Caucasians, Tibetans and others)
type: compilation / comparative linguistics and ethnography (scientific report)
language: German (with vocabularies in many languages, Latin transcription) (original: German)

date.subject_text: 1805-1808 (own fieldwork); vocabularies from the eighteenth century

regions_text: all of Asia: Siberia, Mongolia, Manchuria, Central Asia, Caucasus, Tibet, China
peoples_text: Mongols; Kalmyks; Buryats; Tungus; Manchus; Turkic peoples (Tatars, Kazakhs, Yakuts, Uighurs); Samoyeds; Finno-Ugrians; Caucasian peoples; Tibetans; Chinese
evidence_text: compilation of vocabularies from earlier collectors (Pallas, Strahlenberg, Messerschmidt, Fischer, the 1787 Vocabularia comparativa) and from Klaproth's own fieldwork on the Siberian-Mongol frontier 1805-1806 and in the Caucasus 1807-1808, with historical extracts from Chinese and other Asian sources
cautions: Vocabularies are second-hand for most languages; Klaproth's Chinese historical extracts are his own translations and have been criticized. Paris imprint by a German author writing in German (eligible as German-language original).
research_value: Klaproth's classification replaced the loose Tartar category with linguistically defined Turkic, Mongol and Tungus families and traced the historical Tatars through Chinese sources; a key document for how the term Tartary was dismantled in nineteenth-century scholarship.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (439 images)

creator: Carl Friedrich von Ledebour, with C. A. Meyer and A. von Bunge
title: Journey through the Altai Mountains and the Zungharian Kirghiz Steppe, undertaken in 1826 at the expense of the Imperial University of Dorpat, 2 parts with plates and maps (Berlin 1829-1830)
regions_text: Altai; Bukhtarma; upper Irtysh; Zungharian (Semipalatinsk) steppe; Kolyvan mines; Qing frontier posts
peoples_text: Kazakhs (Kirghiz of the Middle Horde); Altai Kalmyks (Telengits); Russian mining administration; Qing frontier (Chuguchak trade)
evidence_text: firsthand observation 1826 in the Russian Altai, the Bukhtarma and Irtysh and the Kazakh (Kirghiz) steppe on the Qing frontier; part 2 contains Meyer's and Bunge's separate journals
cautions: Three authors; part 2 journals by Meyer and Bunge are separately attributable. Multiple duplicated Google copies with inconsistent volume tagging.
research_value: Eyewitness account of the Altai frontier zone between the Russian mining district and the former Zunghar lands, including the Ablaikit ruins and Kazakh camps; part of the 1820s wave that replaced generalized Tartary with surveyed Kirghiz steppe.
access_status: Open scans + OCR text retrieved

creator: Gustav Rose
title: Journey to the Ural, the Altai and the Caspian Sea, carried out in 1829 by order of the Emperor of Russia by A. von Humboldt, G. Ehrenberg and G. Rose: mineralogical-geognostic part and historical report of the journey, 2 vols (Berlin 1837-1842)
type: travel narrative / scientific report (expedition narrative and geology)
regions_text: Ural; western Siberia; Altai (Kolyvan, Zmeinogorsk); Irtysh to the Qing frontier; Orenburg; Caspian (Astrakhan)
peoples_text: Bashkirs; Kazakhs (Kirghiz); Kalmyks of Astrakhan; Tatars; Russian mining and Cossack administration; Qing frontier post visited from Ust-Kamenogorsk
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Rose's day-by-day narrative of Humboldt's 1829 expedition (Ural, Tobolsk, Barnaul, Altai, Semipalatinsk, Orenburg, Caspian at Astrakhan) with Humboldt's contributions
cautions: Rose is the narrator; Humboldt's letters and observations are interleaved. Humboldt's Asie centrale (1843, French) is outside this tradition.
research_value: The German narrative of Humboldt's Asian journey (Humboldt's own Fragmens and Asie centrale are French); documents the Kazakh steppe, Kalmyk camps and the Chinese frontier at the Irtysh as seen in 1829.
access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved (vol 1); vol 2 present among Google copies but volume assignment not verified

creator: Eduard Eversmann
title: Journey from Orenburg to Bukhara, with a vocabulary of the Afghan language, two plates and the plan of Bukhara (Berlin 1823)
type: travel narrative / scientific report (with linguistic appendix)
language: German (with Russian, Tatar, Pashto and Persian word lists) (original: German)
regions_text: Orenburg; Kazakh steppe; Ust-Urt; Kyzylkum; Bukhara
peoples_text: Kazakhs (Kirghiz-Kaisaks); Karakalpaks; Khiva; Emirate of Bukhara; Turkmens; Afghans (vocabulary)
evidence_text: firsthand observation: Eversmann travelled disguised as a merchant with the Negri mission caravan 1820-1821 through the Kazakh steppe to Bukhara; Klaproth contributed a linguistic note

access_status: Open scan + OCR text retrieved

creator: Alexander Gustav von Schrenk
title: Journey to the Northeast of European Russia, through the Tundras of the Samoyeds, to the Arctic Ural Mountains, undertaken in 1837 for the Imperial Botanical Garden, part 1 (Dorpat 1848)
regions_text: Mezen; Pechora; Bolshezemelskaya tundra; Arctic Ural; Kara Sea approaches
peoples_text: Samoyeds (Nenets); Zyrians (Komi); Russian Pomors
evidence_text: firsthand observation 1837 among the European Samoyeds (Nenets) and at the Arctic Ural, the northern boundary of Siberia
cautions: Part 2 (1854) is post-cutoff publication of the same journey. | Low priority; included because journey date 1837 is in scope.

access_status: Open scan + OCR text available (metadata verified)

creator: Sagang Sechen; I. J. Schmidt (ed. and tr.)
title: History of the Eastern Mongols and their Princely House, composed by Sagang Sechen Khungtaiji of the Ordos (Erdeni-yin tobchi, 1662): Mongolian text with German translation and notes (St Petersburg 1829)
type: chronicle (Mongolian, seventeenth century) in bilingual critical edition
regions_text: Mongolia; Ordos; northern China; Tibet (religious history); Oirat lands
peoples_text: Mongols (Yuan and Northern Yuan khans); Oirats; Tibetan Buddhist hierarchs; Ming and Qing China

regions_text: Whole known world with East at top; Asia including Scythia, India, the Caspian, the Tartar lands of Sanudo's text; Mediterranean and Black Sea portolans
evidence_text: Compilation: portolan-chart coastlines combined with a circular mappamundi of Asia drawn from written sources (Sanudo's crusading treatise), with early Mongol-era information; no observation of Asia by the maker.
cautions: Catalogue (DigiVatLib) attributes the maps to Pietro Vesconte; several Sanudo manuscripts (BL Add MS 27376, Paris, Vatican) carry variants of the same map set, so this copy is one witness among siblings rather than a unique original. research_value: The Vesconte-Sanudo mappamundi is the first Western world map made after the Mongol conquests with a portolan-style frame; it shows the Latin West's early 14th-century picture of Asia at the moment 'Tartari' entered European geography (Sanudo's text discusses Tartar alliances). A companion to the BL Add MS 27376 copy.

creator: Anthony Jenkinson (1562 design); 1914 reproduction issued by the Russian Resettlement Administration in the Atlas Aziatskoi Rossii
title: Description of Russia, Muscovy and Tartary, by Anthony Jenkinson, London 1562 (as reproduced in 1914 with Russian translations of the legends)
type: facsimile (1914 lithographic reproduction of a 16th-century printed map)
regions_text: Russia; Muscovy; Tartaria (across the steppe); Cassackia; Nagaia; Tumen; Colmack; Molgomzaia; Kitaia lacus; Samarcand; Boghar; Taskent; Kirgessi; Mare Caspium; Shamarghan; Media; Persia
evidence_text: Mixed: Jenkinson's own 1558-1560 journey (Moscow, Volga, Caspian, Bukhara) plus informant testimony for Cathay, Kirgiz, Kalmyk (Colmack) and Samoyed regions; the object is a 20th-century reproduction.
cautions: LOC catalogue dates the item 1562 but the object is a 1914 lithographic reproduction 'copied from Jenkinson's map published by V. Kordt' (Materialy po istorii russkoi kartografii). The sole surviving original 1562 London impression is in Wroclaw University Library (identified 1987); reproductions made before that, including Kordt's, follow Ortelius's 1570 reduced plate, so this object should be treated as a witness to the Ortelius state unless compared with the Wroclaw sheet. LOC 'created/published' field contains a garbled machine rendering of the Russian imprint. | Europeana University of Tartu copies of the Ortelius plate to be checked separately (see candidates).
research_value: The Jenkinson map is the first English map of Russia and the first Western map built partly on a Central Asian journey; it spreads TARTARIA over the whole steppe from Crimea to the Ob and Tashkent and records ethnonyms (Cassackia, Colmack, Kirgessi, Nagaia) that later maps copied for two centuries. Its dependence chain (Jenkinson 1562 > Ortelius 1570 > De Jode 1578 > later) is central to the 'Tartaria on maps' question.

cautions: Six known 1602 impressions (Vatican, Kyoto, Miyagi, Minnesota Bell, etc.); Kyoto note records the printer colophon 銭塘張文寿過紙 万暦壬寅孟秋. Ricci's northern Asia is Ortelian, not observed. | Labels read on image 1 region: 歐邏巴, 莫斯哥未亞, 亞細亞, 韃靼, 北高海, 大乃河, 撒馬兒罕, 女人國, 鬼國, 夜叉國, 回回, 沙漠, 大明, 北京, 亞力山的; Arctic text cartouches on the northern peoples.
research_value: The Chinese source of the East Asian Tartary vocabulary: Ricci placed 韃靼 north of the Ming and 莫斯哥未亞 to its west, with 北高海 for the Caspian; every later Chinese and Japanese world map (Verbiest, Nagakubo) repeats these labels, so this is the root object for how Tartary was named in East Asia.

creator: Kwon Kun and Yi Hoe (1402); Ryukoku copy c.1470-1480; Kyoto coloured replica 1910
title: Kangnido (Map of Integrated Lands and Regions of Historical Countries and Capitals), 1402: coloured replica (1910) of the Ryukoku University copy, held by Kyoto University Graduate School of Letters (IIIF)
original_script_title: 混一疆理歷代國都之圖
tradition: Multilingual pass: Islamic, Russian, East Asian and Inner Asian cartography
type: modern reconstruction: 1910 coloured replica of a c.1470-1480 manuscript copy of the 1402 map
regions_text: Eurasia and Africa; Mongolia, Central Asia (with Timurid cities), Arabia, Africa, Europe in outline; Korea enlarged
evidence_text: compilation: Korean synthesis (1402) of two Yuan Chinese maps (Li Zemin's Shengjiao guangbei tu and Qingjun's Hunyi jiangli tu) with Korean and Japanese additions; Inner Asia and the West derive from Mongol-era Islamic knowledge
cautions: A 1910 hand-coloured copy, not the original; Kyoto notes the postface texts were not copied. The Honkoji copy (Shimabara) and Tenri copy are later variants.
research_value: The Kangnido preserves the Mongol-era (Yuan) picture of Inner Asia, Central Asia and the west as known in Korea in 1402, before European Tartary maps existed; the Ryukoku original is not open online, so this faithful 1910 replica is the practical access route.
